The contents include acknowledgments, abbreviations, acronyms, an executive summary, and detailed sections on the rationale, objectives, methods, and recommendations for the prevention, treatment, and management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with a focus on genital herpes simplex virus (HSV). Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are a significant global public health issue, affecting quality of life and causing severe morbidity and mortality. They directly impact reproductive and child health through infertility, cancers, and pregnancy complications, and indirectly facilitate the sexual transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), thereby affecting national and individual economies. Over one million STIs are acquired daily. Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) is the most common cause of genital ulcers in many countries. In 2012, there were approximately 19.2 million new HSV-2 infections among individuals aged 15–49 years globally, with the highest rates among younger age groups. This translates to an estimated 417 million people living with HSV-2 infection in 2012. HSV type 1 (HSV-1) typically causes non-sexually transmitted oral herpes infections but can also be transmitted to the genitals through oral sex. HSV-1 is increasingly recognized as a cause of genital herpes, particularly in high-income countries, with an estimated 140 million people globally having genital HSV-1 infection in 2012. HSV-2 infection is of particular concern due to its epidemiological synergy with HIV infection and transmission. Individuals infected with HSV-2 are approximately three times more likely to acquire HIV, and those co-infected with HIV and genital HSV are more likely to transmit HIV to others. Symptomatic genital HSV is a lifelong condition characterized by frequent symptomatic recurrences. Most initial infections are asymptomatic or atypical, leaving the majority of HSV-2-infected individuals undiagnosed. The classical clinical presentation of primary genital HSV infection includes bilateral clusters of erythematous papules, vesicles, or ulcerations on the external genitalia, perianal region, or buttocks, occurring 4–7 days after sexual exposure. However, this classical syndrome occurs in only 10–25% of primary infections. Although HSV-1 and HSV-2 are usually transmitted via different routes and affect different areas of the body, their signs and symptoms overlap. The first episode of genital HSV-1 infection cannot be clinically differentiated from genital HSV-2 infection; laboratory tests are required for differentiation. When vesicles are absent, laboratory confirmation may be necessary to rule out other causes of genital ulcers. Most individuals will experience one or more symptomatic recurrences within one year after the first symptomatic episode of HSV-2 infection. In contrast, symptomatic episodes are much less likely to recur with genital HSV-1 infection. Symptomatic recurrences are generally less severe than the first episode. Established HSV-2 infection typically leads to intermittent viral shedding from the genital mucosa, even in the absence of symptoms. Since the publication of the 2003 WHO Guidelines for the management of sexually transmitted infections, changes in STI epidemiology and advancements in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment necessitate updates in STI management. These guidelines provide updated treatment recommendations for genital HSV infection based on the most recent evidence. They form one of several modules of guidelines for specific STIs. Other modules will address treatments for Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhea), Chlamydia trachomatis (chlamydial infection), and Treponema pallidum (syphilis). Future work will provide guidance on syphilis screening and treatment in pregnant women, STI syndromic approaches, clinical management, STI prevention, and treatments for other STIs. Countries are strongly encouraged to incorporate updated global guidance into their standardized national protocols, adapting this guidance to local epidemiological situations and antimicrobial susceptibility data. The objectives of these guidelines are: To provide evidence-based guidance on the treatment of genital HSV infection. To support countries in updating their national guidelines for the treatment of genital HSV infection. These guidelines were developed following the methods outlined in the 2014 WHO handbook for guideline development. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included international STI experts, clinicians, researchers, and program managers. The GDG prioritized questions and outcomes related to the treatment of genital HSV infections for inclusion in this update. A methodologist and a team of systematic reviewers from McMaster University, the WHO Collaborating Centre for Evidence-Informed Policy, independently conducted systematic reviews of the effectiveness of different treatments for genital HSV infections. The evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach and presented to the GDG. Conflicts of interest were managed according to WHO guidelines and declared before the recommendations were discussed and finalized. Research implications were also developed by the GDG. For adults and adolescents with a first clinical episode of genital HSV infection, the WHO STI guideline recommends treatment over no treatment. A strong recommendation is made based on moderate-quality evidence. The guideline suggests a standard dose of acyclovir over valaciclovir or famciclovir. Dosages include: Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 10 days (standard dose). Acyclovir 200 mg orally five times daily for 10 days. Valaciclovir 500 mg orally twice daily for 10 days. Famciclovir 250 mg orally three times daily for 10 days. Given that follow-up visits may not be possible during treatment and symptoms of the first clinical episode may be prolonged, therapy is provided for 10 days. Although the benefits of the medicines are likely similar, the costs of valaciclovir and famciclovir are higher than acyclovir, making acyclovir the preferred choice. The choice of medicine may also depend on compliance considerations. For adults and adolescents with recurrent clinical episodes of genital HSV infection, the WHO STI guideline suggests treatment over no treatment. Treatment should be initiated within the first 24 hours of symptom onset or during the prodromal phase.
